title: Willow fruit bowl
subtitle: A shallow open bowl for the kitchen table
excerpt: A willow fruit bowl: 28 cm diameter, 8 cm deep, made entirely from buff willow in a round-slath base and randed sides. The wider spacing and tighter weavers give it a more sculptural look than a bread basket, and the shallow form shows the fruit.

glossaryTerms.definition: The upright structural rods of a basket that form the frame for the woven sides. Stakes are heavier-gauge rods than weavers.
The crossed-stick foundation of a round basket base. Two groups of sticks are pierced and interlocked to form the cross.
A pointed steel spike used to open up the weave to insert new rods or to thread the border work.
A single-rod weave, going in front of one stake and behind one stake alternately. The simplest weave structure.

content.text: A willow fruit bowl is shallower and wider relative to its diameter than a bread basket. At 8 cm deep and 28 cm across, the flare of the sides is more pronounced, which opens up the form and makes the fruit visible from above. The construction uses an eight-stick
base in buff willow, with 16 side
(single-rod weave) for the sides rather than pairing. Randing with 16 stakes requires an odd number of stakes; 17 stakes are used so that the single-rod weave spirals correctly.
Base sticks: 8 buff willow rods, 32 cm, 7 mm at butt. Stakes: 17 buff willow rods, 55 cm, 6 mm at butt. Weavers: 50 buff willow rods, 90 cm to 1 m, 3 to 4 mm at butt.
Step 1: Make and open the slath

and thread the other four through. Pairing-weave the cross for three rounds treating groups of four as single units, then open to individual sticks and pair for a further four rounds. The base diameter is 20 cm at this stage.

Slype and insert 16 stakes (two per base stick, one per side), then add one extra stake beside any base stick to bring the total to 17. 17 is the required odd number for a single-rod randing weave with no second rod needed. Fold stakes upward and upset with two rounds of pairing weave.

Insert a single buff rod and weave in front of one stake, behind one stake, all the way around. Because there are 17 (odd) stakes, the weave automatically alternates sides on each revolution without a second rod. Rand to 7 cm height. The wider spacing between stakes in randing compared to pairing gives the open, airy look of a fruit bowl.
Weave two rounds of three-rod wale at the rim. Work a simple three-rod behind-one border. On a shallow bowl the border stakes are short; angle the bodkin to find the tuck-under point.

attrs.symptom: The randing weave is not alternating correctly, ending in the same place each round
attrs.cause: An even number of stakes was used instead of 17 (odd).
attrs.fix: Count the stakes before starting to rand. If an even number was inserted, add one extra stake before continuing.

attrs.symptom: The sides are pulling inward rather than flaring
attrs.cause: The randing tension is too tight, or the stakes are too straight upright.
attrs.fix: Press the stakes outward to the correct angle (about 20 degrees from vertical for a fruit bowl) with one hand while weaving with the other. Use a former (a round pot or bowl) inside to hold the shape during the first five rounds.
